title: Take-Home Exercises: Going Deeper
text:
WarningRead This Later, Not During the Workshop



The three exercises below are optional enrichment — we do not cover them live. They preview the R code from Sessions 3–4 against a practice server and go deeper into error handling. Nothing in the live sessions depends on them; work through them at your own pace after the workshop.
These exercises originally lived at the end of Session 2 — The Anatomy of a Request. They are also a good place to practice building functions yourself — during the workshop you mostly used pre-built code, and here you get to write some from scratch.

title: Take-Home Exercises: Going Deeper
section: Exercise A: Under the Hood — What Happens When You Make a Request
text:
Exercise A: Under the Hood — What Happens When You Make a Request
Let’s connect everything together:

You construct a URL from a base URL (endpoint) + query string (parameters).
Your client sends a GET request using this URL to the API.
The API relays this request to the server.
The server processes the request, queries the database, and sends a response.
The response includes a status code and the requested data (formatted as JSON).
Your R code parses the JSON into a data structure you can work with.







ImportantCommon Misconception



We are not sending JSON when we make a GET request. We’re sending a URL with parameters. JSON is what comes back to us in the response.

title: Take-Home Exercises: Going Deeper
section: Exercise B: Making Requests to a Dummy Server in R
text:
Exercise B: Making Requests to a Dummy Server in R
These blocks show real requests to a practice server. You can run them any time after the workshop.

library(httr2)       # Makes web requests
library(tibble)      # Tidyverse data frames
library(dplyr)       # Data manipulation
library(glue)        # String construction

A simple GET request to a public test API:

# Step 1: Define the URL
test_url <- "https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users/1"

# Step 2: Create a request object
req <- request(test_url)

# Step 3: Perform the request
response <- req_perform(req)

# Step 4: Check the status code
resp_status(response)

# Step 5: Check the content type
resp_content_type(response)


# Step 6: Parse the JSON response
result <- resp_body_json(response)

# Step 7: Inspect the structure
str(result)


# Step 8: Convert to a data frame
user_df <- as.data.frame(result)
print(user_df)

A GET request with query parameters:

# Get posts by a specific user
posts_url <- "https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts"

posts_url_query <- glue("{posts_url}?userId=1")

req <- request(posts_url_query)
response <- req_perform(req)

if (resp_status(response) == 200) {
  posts <- resp_body_json(response)
  cat("Number of posts retrieved:", length(posts), "\n")
}

And a POST request — sending data to the server:

# Step 1: Define the endpoint
post_url <- "https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts"

# Step 2: Create the request with a body
req <- request(post_url) |>
  req_method("POST") |>
  req_headers("Content-Type" = "application/json") |>
  req_body_json(list(
    title = "My API Workshop Post",
    body = "Learning about APIs is fun!",
    userId = 1
  ))

# Step 3: Perform the request
response <- req_perform(req)

# Step 4: Check the status code (201 = Created)
cat("Status:", resp_status(response), "\n")

# Step 5: See the response
result <- resp_body_json(response)
print(result)







NoteStatus Code 201



Notice we got a 201 Created instead of 200 OK. This is the standard success code for POST requests — it means the server successfully created the new resource.

section: Exercise 1: Astronomy Picture of the Day
text:
Exercise 1: Astronomy Picture of the Day
The APOD endpoint returns a single JSON object describing today’s featured image or video, along with a scientific explanation written by a professional astronomer.

apod_url <- glue("https://api.nasa.gov/planetary/apod?api_key={nasa_key}")

req      <- request(apod_url)
response <- req_perform(req)

# Always check the status first
resp_status(response)


apod <- resp_body_json(response)

# Inspect the top-level keys
names(apod)


cat("Title:     ", apod$title,      "\n")
cat("Date:      ", apod$date,       "\n")
cat("Media type:", apod$media_type, "\n")
cat("URL:       ", apod$url,        "\n")
cat("\nExplanation:\n", apod$explanation, "\n")


Challenge A — Request a Specific Date
Add a date query parameter to retrieve any past APOD. Dates go back to 1995-06-16.

apod_dated_url <- glue(
  "https://api.nasa.gov/planetary/apod",
  "?api_key={nasa_key}&date=1995-06-16"
)

apod_first <- resp_body_json(req_perform(request(apod_dated_url)))
cat("First ever APOD:", apod_first$title, "\n")



Challenge B — Retrieve a Batch of APODs
Use the count parameter to retrieve multiple random APODs in a single request.

apod_batch_url <- glue(
  "https://api.nasa.gov/planetary/apod",
  "?api_key={nasa_key}&count=5"
)

apod_list <- resp_body_json(req_perform(request(apod_batch_url)))

# How is the structure different from a single APOD?
length(apod_list)
apod_list[[1]]$title

title: Practice Lab 1: NASA Open APIs
text:
Exercise 2: Near-Earth Object (Asteroid) Data
The NEO endpoint returns every asteroid that passed near Earth within a date range. The response is nested three levels deep — a great exercise in list navigation.

neo_url <- glue(
  "https://api.nasa.gov/neo/rest/v1/feed",
  "?start_date=2024-01-01&end_date=2024-01-07",
  "&api_key={nasa_key}"
)

response <- req_perform(request(neo_url))
neo_data <- resp_body_json(response)

cat("Total asteroids in this range:", neo_data$element_count, "\n")
cat("Top-level keys:", paste(names(neo_data), collapse=", "), "\n")


# Near-Earth objects are nested: neo_data$near_earth_objects → date → list of asteroids
dates <- names(neo_data$near_earth_objects)
cat("Dates in response:", paste(dates, collapse=", "), "\n")

# Look at the first asteroid on the first date
first_day   <- neo_data$near_earth_objects[[dates[1]]]
first_rock  <- first_day[[1]]

cat("Name:", first_rock$name, "\n")
cat("Hazardous?", first_rock$is_potentially_hazardous_asteroid, "\n")
cat("Min diameter (km):",
    first_rock$estimated_diameter$kilometers$estimated_diameter_min, "\n")


# Flatten all dates and asteroids into a single data frame
all_asteroids <- lapply(neo_data$near_earth_objects, function(day) {
  lapply(day, function(rock) {
    data.frame(
      name          = rock$name,
      date          = rock$close_approach_data[[1]]$close_approach_date,
      is_hazardous  = rock$is_potentially_hazardous_asteroid,
      min_diam_km   = rock$estimated_diameter$kilometers$estimated_diameter_min,
      max_diam_km   = rock$estimated_diameter$kilometers$estimated_diameter_max,
      miss_dist_km  = as.numeric(rock$close_approach_data[[1]]$miss_distance$kilometers),
      speed_kmh     = as.numeric(rock$close_approach_data[[1]]$relative_velocity$kilometers_per_hour)
    )
  }) |> bind_rows()
}) |> bind_rows()

glimpse(all_asteroids)


ggplot(all_asteroids, aes(x = miss_dist_km / 1e6, fill = is_hazardous)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 25, alpha = 0.85, color = "white") +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("FALSE" = "#4f46e5", "TRUE" = "#ef4444"),
    labels = c("Not Hazardous", "Potentially Hazardous")
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Asteroid Miss Distances — Jan 1–7, 2024",
    subtitle = "Each bar = one asteroid; distance from Earth's center",
    x        = "Miss Distance (millions of km)",
    y        = "Count",
    fill     = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

text:
Questions

———————


Q1.
(Conceptual): In this lab the API key is passed as a query parameter (?api_key=...). Name one situation where this approach could create a security risk.






TipAnswer Q1





The key is visible in the URL — which means it appears in browser history, server access logs, and anywhere the URL is copy-pasted or shared. If you accidentally post the URL in a public place (a GitHub issue, a Slack message, a screenshot), your key is exposed. Header-based auth keeps the credential out of the URL entirely.




———————


———————



Q2.
(Code): The count parameter returns a list of APODs instead of a single object. Write code that extracts just the title from each item in the batch and prints them as a character vector.






TipAnswer Q2





titles <- sapply(apod_list, function(x) x$title)

The GitHub REST API is the most realistic example in this workshop — it is a production API used by millions of developers daily. It introduces two concepts you haven’t seen yet:

No-auth public access — many endpoints work without any credential, though with strict rate limits
Fine-grained Personal Access Tokens (PATs) — scoped tokens where you explicitly choose what permissions to grant

The PAT exercise is a live demonstration of least-privilege security: only give a credential exactly the access it needs, and nothing more.
Auth patterns: None (public) → Bearer token with Authorization: Bearer TOKEN.

Exercise 3: Create a Fine-Grained Personal Access Token

Step 3a — Create the Token

Go to github.com → your avatar → Settings
Scroll to Developer Settings → Personal Access Tokens → Fine-grained tokens
Click Generate new token
Set:

Token name: api-workshop-lab
Expiration: 7 days
Resource owner: your account
Repository access: Public repositories only
Permissions: Metadata → Read-only (this is the minimum needed)

Click Generate token and copy it immediately — it won’t be shown again
Add it to your .Renviron:

GITHUB_TOKEN=your_token_here






ImportantWhat You Just Did



You created a token with the minimum necessary permissions: read access to metadata on public repositories only. Even if this token leaked, an attacker could only read public data — they could not write code, delete repositories, or access private data. This is the principle of least privilege.

text:
Questions

———————


Q1.
(Conceptual): In Exercise 1, you saw the x-ratelimit-remaining header in the response. Why would an API designer include rate limit information in the response headers rather than (or in addition to) the response body?






TipAnswer Q1





Headers deliver metadata about the response — information about the exchange itself, not the data you requested. Putting rate limit info in headers keeps the response body clean and focused on the requested data. It also means client code can check rate limits without parsing the body — a faster, more efficient check. This is the standard HTTP convention: data goes in the body, metadata goes in headers.




———————


———————



Q2.
(Security): You created a fine-grained token with read-only access to public repositories. Describe a scenario where even this minimal token could be misused if it leaked publicly.






TipAnswer Q2





An attacker with a public-read token could: - Scrape your public repository data at the 5,000 req/hour authenticated rate (vs. 60/hour unauthenticated) — useful for mass enumeration - Identify which public repos you contribute to, revealing professional affiliations or project work you hadn’t publicized - Burn through your rate limit, causing your own API calls to fail
This is why even minimal tokens should be rotated (deleted and regenerated) quickly if leaked, and why expiry dates are important — a 7-day token automatically becomes useless.




———————


———————



Q3.
(Extension): Modify the repository search from Exercise 2 to collect all pages of results (not just the first 20). GitHub limits search results to 1,000 total — use total_count and per_page to calculate how many pages to fetch, and use Sys.sleep(1) between requests to avoid hitting rate limits.






TipAnswer Q3





search_all_github <- function(query, token, max_results = 100) {
  per_page   <- 30
  total_pages <- ceiling(min(max_results, 1000) / per_page)

  all_results <- lapply(seq_len(total_pages), function(p) {
    Sys.sleep(1)  # be a polite client
    req <- request("https://api.github.com/search/repositories") |>
      req_headers(
        Authorization = glue("Bearer {token}"),
        Accept        = "application/vnd.github+json",
        `User-Agent`  = "API-Workshop-Student"
      ) |>
      req_url_query(q = query, sort = "stars", per_page = per_page, page = p)

    data <- resp_body_json(req_perform(req))
    lapply(data$items, function(r) {
      data.frame(name = r$full_name, stars = r$stargazers_count, language = r$language %||% NA)
    }) |> bind_rows()
  }) |> bind_rows()

  all_results
}
Sys.sleep(1) adds a 1-second pause between pages. This is good API citizenship — it avoids triggering abuse detection and spreads requests over time.




———————

Part 1: Historical Weather — The Full ETV Pipeline

Look First
Open-Meteo’s archive endpoint returns past weather. Inspect this URL before copying or running it: predict the city, dates, variables, and units.
https://archive-api.open-meteo.com/v1/archive?latitude=35.28&longitude=-120.66&start_date=2025-07-01&end_date=2025-07-07&daily=temperature_2m_max,temperature_2m_min&temperature_unit=fahrenheit&timezone=auto
You’ll see a JSON body whose daily object holds three parallel arrays — dates, daily highs, daily lows.


Now in Words
The endpoint is https://archive-api.open-meteo.com/v1/archive — a third door, following the same convention as Session 3’s forecast and geocoding doors. Two new query parameters do the date work: start_date and end_date. And here’s the good news — one request returns the entire date range. No loops needed.
Now the full pipeline in R, pre-built: geocode the city name → request the historical data → build the data frame. In your workshop file, the only blanks are the city name and the two dates — everything structural is written for you:

# Step 0 — Geocode: city name → coordinates (Session 3's endpoint)
city_name <- "San Luis Obispo"

geo <- request("https://geocoding-api.open-meteo.com/v1/search") |>
  req_url_query(name = city_name, count = 1) |>
  req_perform() |>
  resp_body_json()

hit <- geo$results[[1]]
my_lat <- round(hit$latitude, 2)
my_lon <- round(hit$longitude, 2)

# E: extract — historical request ---------------------------
result <- request("https://archive-api.open-meteo.com/v1/archive") |>
  req_url_query(
    latitude = my_lat,
    longitude = my_lon,
    start_date = "2025-07-01",
    end_date = "2025-07-07",
    daily = "temperature_2m_max,temperature_2m_min",
    temperature_unit = "fahrenheit",
    timezone = "auto"
  ) |>
  req_perform() |>
  resp_body_json()

# Peek at the daily piece
str(result$daily, max.level = 1)

The daily element is a named list of three parallel lists: time, temperature_2m_max, and temperature_2m_min — one entry per day.

# T: transform ------------------------------------------------
slo_df <- tibble(
  city     = city_name,
  date     = as.Date(unlist(result$daily$time)),
  temp_max = unlist(result$daily$temperature_2m_max),
  temp_min = unlist(result$daily$temperature_2m_min)
)




Show historical-data table


slo_df









NoteWhy unlist()?



resp_body_json() parses each JSON array into an R list. unlist() flattens that list into a plain vector, which is what a tibble column needs. List in, vector out — that’s all it does.



———————



Q1.
(Fill in the Blank): To ask the archive endpoint for a different range of days, we change the ________ and ________ query parameters.






TipAnswer Q1





start_date and end_date. Everything else in the request can stay exactly the same.




———————


———————



Q2.
(Multiple Choice): What does unlist() do in the Transform step?

It flattens a list into a plain vector so it can be a tibble column.
It sends the request to the server.
It removes missing values from the data.
It converts Fahrenheit to Celsius.
It sorts the dates in order.







TipAnswer Q2





a) JSON arrays arrive in R as lists; unlist() turns each one into a vector — exactly what tibble columns are made of.




———————

Part 4: Reflection, Classroom Applications & Survey

———————


Q7.
(Discussion): You just built a complete data pipeline: API request → JSON parsing → data wrangling → visualization. Think about the courses you teach. Where could API data naturally integrate into your curriculum? What topics could benefit from live, real-world data?






TipExample Answers





Possible integration points:

Intro Stats: Use weather data for descriptive statistics (mean temperature, variability across cities)
Regression: Model temperature as a function of latitude or time
Data Wrangling: Parse nested JSON, clean and reshape API responses
Probability: Explore weather prediction accuracy (forecast vs. actual)
Capstone Projects: Let students choose an API and build their own data pipeline





———————



Common Pitfalls When Working with APIs

Rate Limits: Most APIs limit how many requests you can make per minute/hour (Open-Meteo’s free tier allows ~10,000 calls/day — generous, but not infinite). Design your code to respect limits.
API Keys (elsewhere): Most commercial APIs require keys. When you use one, never write the key directly in your script — store it in an environment file. The Practice Labs on this site walk through this.
Data Structure Changes: API providers can change their response format without warning. Always inspect the structure of new responses (str()) before building pipelines around them.
URL Encoding: Special characters (spaces, ampersands, accents) must be encoded in URLs. req_url_query() handles this for you automatically — one more reason to like it.
Nested JSON Complexity: Real-world JSON can be deeply nested. Practice with str() and names() to navigate the structure before trying to flatten it.



Reflection Questions for Your Practice

Where could API data naturally integrate into your curriculum?
What are the pitfalls (rate limits, authentication) that students need to know?
How does working with live, messy data differ from working with pre-cleaned datasets?
What ethical considerations arise when collecting data from APIs?

text:
Part 1: The CRUD Framework

Watch First
Step through the four operations with the buttons — one quadrant lights up at a time.
What to notice: each operation pairs one verb (what you want done) with one HTTP method (how you say it) — and one of the four quadrants is where data scientists spend nearly all their time. See if you can guess which before the last step.

  
    
      ➕CreatePOSTadd something new
    
    
      👁️ReadGETlook at existing data
    
    
      ✏️UpdatePUT / PATCHedit something
    
    
      🗑️DeleteDELETEremove it
    
  
  
  
    ⏮ Restart
    ◀ Back
    
    Next ▶
    ▶ Play
  





Now in Words
What type of client requests can we make? The CRUD framework organizes the four fundamental operations. The animation maps each CRUD operation to a visual icon: a plus sign for Create/POST (adding something new), an eye for Read/GET (looking at existing data), a pencil for Update/PUT-PATCH (editing something), and a trash can for Delete/DELETE (removing it).



CRUD Operation
HTTP Method
Description




Create
POST
Submit new data to the server


Read
GET
Retrieve existing data from the server


Update
PUT / PATCH
Modify existing data on the server


Delete
DELETE
Remove a resource from the server









Important📖 Definition — HTTP



HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) is the standard set of rules for sending requests and responses across the web. The methods in the table — GET, POST, PUT, DELETE — are HTTP’s built-in verbs: they announce what kind of action a request is asking for.








NoteFor Data Science



In data science, Read (GET) is by far the most common operation. We’re typically pulling data, not writing to databases. As a data scientist, the eye (Read/GET) quadrant will cover the vast majority of your API work.








Tip🎯 Goal Check



Our workshop goal — make a request, format the response — lives almost entirely in the Read (GET) quadrant. Everything we do tomorrow is a GET.



———————



Visual Check — CRUD Operations.
(Multiple Choice): A social media app lets users edit their display name. Based on the animation above, which CRUD operation and HTTP method does that action map to?

Create — POST
Read — GET
Delete — DELETE
Update — PUT/PATCH
Read — POST







TipAnswer — Visual Check





d) Update — PUT/PATCH. Editing an existing record (changing a name that already exists) is an Update operation — the pencil icon. It is not Create (nothing new is being added) or Read (data is being changed, not just viewed).




———————


———————



Q1.
(Fill in the Blank): The HTTP method used to read (retrieve) data from a server is ________.






TipAnswer Q1





GET. Read = GET, and it is by far the most common operation in data science API work.




———————


———————



Q2.
(Multiple Choice): Which CRUD operation is most commonly used in data science when working with APIs?

Read
Create
Update
Delete
All four equally







TipAnswer Q2





a) Read. Data scientists most commonly use GET requests to read (retrieve) data from external sources. We’re consumers of data, not typically writing to external databases.




———————

title: Session 2: The Anatomy of a Request
text:
Part 2: GET & POST Requests
A GET request is all about retrieving data. You’re asking the server: “Give me this information.”

Watch First
Step through the GET request at your own pace — Next, Back, or press Play.



Now in Words
The animation shows a GET request for the resource GET /users/42. The request originates at the Client and travels through the API to the Server and Database. Notice two things: first, the request carries only a path (/users/42) — no data payload. Second, the response brings data back to the client while nothing new is written to the database.
Here is the flow of a GET request:

Client constructs a request for a resource.
API receives and validates the client’s request.
Server locates the requested data within the database.
Client receives the requested data from the server.







NoteGET Characteristics




The request parameters are encoded in the URL (visible in the address bar)
GET requests are meant to be read-only — they don’t change data on the server
They are idempotent — making the same request multiple times gives the same result









Tip🎯 Goal Check



“Make a request” in our goal sentence means, concretely: send a GET request — a URL asking for data.



———————



Visual Check — GET Request.
(Fill in the Blank): The animation shows GET /users/42. If you changed the request to GET /users/7, the only thing that changes is the ________ — the method, the flow, and everything else stay the same.






TipAnswer — Visual Check





The path (specifically, the number identifying which user you want — 42 becomes 7). The HTTP method is still GET and the flow (client → API → server → database → back) is identical.




———————


———————



Q3.
(Multiple Choice): Which of the following is an example of a task a data scientist would do with a GET request?

Deleting old records from a company database
Uploading a new profile photo
Posting a comment on a forum
Changing your account password
Retrieving the top 10 most popular articles from the New York Times API







TipAnswer Q3





e) Retrieving articles is reading existing data — a GET. The other four options all change something on the server (delete, create, create, update).




———————



POST Requests (Optional)
A POST request is about sending new data to the server. You’re telling the server: “Here’s something new — store it.”
Live decision, based on time: everything we do tomorrow is GET, so this is a flex. Pick a tab — the quick version takes one minute; the full walkthrough about ten.

⏭ Quick Version (~1 min)📮 Full Walkthrough (~10 min)


One idea is enough: POST sends new data to the server, and that data travels in the request body — unlike GET, which carries everything in the URL and only asks for data.
Think of it this way: GET is borrowing a book from the library. POST is donating a new book to it.
That’s all this workshop needs — if we skipped the details today, come back to the Full Walkthrough tab after the workshop.



Watch First
Step through the POST request — watch where the payload starts and where it ends up.



Now in Words
The animation shows a POST request sending POST /users with a JSON payload { "name": "Maya", "email": "maya@example.com" }. Compare this carefully to the GET animation: with GET, data flowed from the server to the client. With POST, data originates at the client and moves toward the server. The client is the source; the server is the destination.
Here is the flow of a POST request:

Client sends new data within the request body.
API receives and validates the client’s new data.
Server creates a new record in the database.
Client receives a confirmation for the new record.







ImportantGET vs. POST — Key Difference




GET sends parameters in the URL — you’re asking for data.
POST sends data in the request body — you’re submitting new data.

Think of it this way: GET is reading a book from the library. POST is donating a new book to the library.




———————


Visual Check — POST Request.
(Multiple Choice): In the POST animation, the JSON payload { "name": "Maya", ... } travels from the Client to the Server. Where does this data live in the request?

In the URL query string, just like GET parameters.
In the request body — unlike GET, which puts parameters in the URL.
In a separate file attachment.
In the status code.
In the database before the request is even sent.







TipAnswer — Visual Check





b) POST sends data in the request body — a separate payload attached to the request. GET requests have no body; all their parameters are encoded directly in the URL (visible in the address bar).





———————


———————


Q4.
(Multiple Choice): Which of the following data science tasks would most likely require a POST request instead of a GET request?

Retrieving the current temperature for a city.
Getting a list of your public repositories from the GitHub API.
Submitting a new tweet through the X (formerly Twitter) API.
Looking up the coordinates for a specific address.
Downloading yesterday’s stock prices.







TipAnswer Q4





c) Submitting a new tweet involves creating a new resource on the server, which is the primary purpose of a POST request. The other options involve only retrieving existing data.





———————


———————


Q5.
(Multiple Choice — Callback to the restaurant analogy): If a GET request is like reading the menu and placing an order, what would a POST request be most analogous to?

Submitting a new recipe for the kitchen to keep in its collection
Asking the waiter to repeat the specials
Paying the bill with exact change
Ordering the same dish twice
Reading the menu a second time







TipAnswer Q5





a) A POST adds something new to the restaurant’s collection — like submitting a new recipe. Options b, d, and e are all just reading/asking again (GET-like), and paying the bill doesn’t add new data to the kitchen.





———————










Tip🎯 Goal Check



POST is good to recognize, but our goal only needs GET. Whichever tab we took, nothing tomorrow depends on POST.

text:
Part 3: URL Anatomy
So how do we actually construct a request? A request is defined by a URL — let’s watch one get taken apart.

Watch First
Step through the URL piece by piece — each click highlights the next component.
What to notice: the address side of the URL has exactly three pieces — protocol, base URL, endpoint — and together they read as one address. Then a ? flips the URL into a different mode entirely. Watch for that flip.



Now in Words
The animation shows the Client (left) and API Server (right) with the URL being broken down between them. Say it out loud, left to right, the same way the animation reveals it:

Protocol — https:// — how to communicate (the s means secure).
Base URL — api.open-meteo.com — which server to talk to; the API’s home address.
Endpoint — /v1/forecast — which resource on that server you want.
Then the ? — and everything after it is the query string: key-value pairs, chained with &, that customize the request.

The first three pieces — protocol, base URL, endpoint — read together as one address: everything to the left of the ?. That’s where the request goes. Everything to the right of the ? is what you’re asking for.






Important📖 Definition — URL



A URL (Uniform Resource Locator) is a web address: a single string of text that says exactly where a resource lives and how to reach it. For API work this matters doubly, because the URL is the request — everything we ask for is encoded in that one string.


Every request URL has two halves:

The address (protocol + base URL + endpoint) — the stable part
The query string (key-value pairs that customize the request) — the dynamic part



Breaking Down a URL
Here is a real URL we will use tomorrow — it asks the free Open-Meteo weather API for the current temperature in San Luis Obispo. Click Next to light up one piece at a time:

  
    https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude=35.28&longitude=-120.66&current=temperature_2m&temperature_unit=fahrenheit
  
  
     Protocol
     Base URL
     Endpoint
     Separators ? &
     Key-value pairs
  
  
  
    ⏮ Restart
    ◀ Back
    
    Next ▶
    ▶ Play
  



And the same anatomy, condensed to five pieces:










Component
Value
Purpose




🟣
Protocol
https://
How — secure communication


🔵
Base URL
api.open-meteo.com
Who — the API server


🟠
Endpoint
/v1/forecast
What resource — the stable part


🔴
Separators
? then &
? starts the customization; & chains pairs


🟢
Key-value pairs
latitude=35.28, …
The details — where, what data, which units









NoteFrom Here On: Watch the Endpoint



Now that you’ve met all three address pieces, here’s the simplification: the protocol and base URL almost never change — every Open-Meteo request in this workshop starts with https://api.open-meteo.com. From this point forward, when you look at a URL, let your eyes jump straight to the endpoint and the query string — that’s where the meaning lives.








NoteKey Vocabulary




An endpoint is the path where an API resource can be accessed (e.g., /v1/forecast) — the stable part of the URL that doesn’t change from one request to the next.
A query string customizes the request using key-value pairs. It always starts with ? and pairs are separated by &.









NoteWhat About API Keys?



Many APIs require one extra query parameter: an API key (e.g., &appid=YOUR_KEY) — an ID that says who is making the request. The Open-Meteo API we use in this workshop is free and does not need a key, so our URLs stay short and simple. Just know the concept exists — you’ll see it in other APIs’ documentation.








Tip🎯 Goal Check



This is the “make a request” half of our goal, fully unpacked: a request = endpoint + query string. Tomorrow we paste this exact URL into a browser and into R.



———————



Visual Check — URL Anatomy.
(Fill in the Blanks): One character each.

The character that marks the boundary between the endpoint and the query string is ____.
The character that separates one key-value pair from the next is ____.







TipAnswer — Visual Check






The ? — everything before it is the stable address; everything after it is customization.
The & — it chains multiple key-value pairs together.





———————


———————



Q6.
(Short Answer): In the URL https://api.spotify.com/v1/search?q=Daft+Punk&type=artist, identify the endpoint and the two key-value pairs that make up the query string.






TipAnswer Q6






Endpoint: /v1/search — the path after the base URL (api.spotify.com)
Key-Value Pairs: q=Daft+Punk and type=artist

(Full anatomy, for the record: protocol https://, base URL api.spotify.com, endpoint /v1/search, then the query string. But your eyes should go straight to the endpoint and the pairs.)




———————

section: Part 4: Putting It Together + Hands-On Preview
text:
Part 4: Putting It Together + Hands-On Preview

Look First — The Whole Journey on One Line
Everything from Sessions 1 and 2 fits in a single picture:
        you build this ↓                                    ↓ you read this
  ┌─────────────────────────────┐                 ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │ GET  endpoint + ?query      │  ── request ──▶ │ 200 + JSON body          │
  │ (the verb)   (the URL)      │  ◀─ response ── │ (status)  (data + meta)  │
  └─────────────────────────────┘                 └──────────────────────────┘
   Client ──▶ API ──▶ Server ──▶ Database ──▶ Server ──▶ API ──▶ Client


Now in Words
You now hold every piece of the request half of our goal:

The verb (Part 1–2): for data work, almost always GET
The sentence (Part 3): a URL — endpoint + ? + key-value pairs chained by &
The reply (Session 1): a JSON body with data, metadata, and a status code

Tomorrow morning we hand this exact recipe to a browser, then to R. Before that, let’s make sure the pieces are locked in.

———————



Q7.
(Multiple Choice — Callback to Session 1): When your R script makes a GET request to a weather API, which statement is correct?

Your script sends JSON and receives a URL.
Your script sends JSON and receives JSON.
Your script sends a URL and receives a URL.
Your script sends a URL and receives JSON.
Your script sends a data frame and receives a plot.







TipAnswer Q7





d) The request itself is a carefully constructed URL containing the endpoint and query parameters. The API’s response comes back as JSON containing the data, metadata, and status code.




———————


———————



Q8.
(Ordering — Preview of tomorrow’s R workflow): Put the following steps in the correct order for making an API request in R. Write the letters in order. (You’ll meet the function names tomorrow — the order is what you already know.)

Parse the JSON response into a data frame
Construct the URL with endpoint and query parameters
Check the status code for success (200)
Send the request using req_perform()
Create a request object with request()







TipAnswer Q8





b → e → d → c → a

b) Construct the URL with endpoint and query parameters
e) Create a request object with request()
d) Send the request using req_perform()
c) Check the status code for success (200)
a) Parse the JSON response into a data frame

(In practice, request() + req_url_query() do steps b and e together.)




———————



Activity — Write a URL on Paper.
No computer for this one. On paper, write the URL that asks Open-Meteo for the current temperature in your hometown, in Fahrenheit. The protocol and base URL are given — they never change. You only fill in the endpoint and the query string (look up your hometown’s rough latitude and longitude on your phone, or ask us):
https://api.open-meteo.com/________?latitude=________&longitude=________&current=________&temperature_unit=fahrenheit
Check yourself against Part 3: endpoint first, ? once, key-value pairs chained with &.






TipOne Possible Answer — Chicago





https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude=41.88&longitude=-87.63&current=temperature_2m&temperature_unit=fahrenheit
The blank that identifies the resource is the endpoint, /v1/forecast; the two that identify where are your latitude and longitude; the one that says what is temperature_2m. Tomorrow you will paste your paper URL into a real browser — keep it!









Tip🎯 Goal Check



You just wrote a complete API request by hand. Tomorrow’s first move is pasting it into a browser and watching a real server answer you.

title: Glossary
text: Quick reference for every term we use across the four sessions. Each entry notes where the term is first introduced, so you can jump back to the full explanation.

title: Glossary
text:
The Cast — Who’s Involved
API (Application Programming Interface) — a structured way for one piece of software to request data or services from another; an agreed-upon set of rules that lets programs talk to each other without either needing to know how the other works inside. In the restaurant analogy: the waiter. (Session 1, Part 1)
Client — the program making the request: your R script, your browser, an app. In the analogy: you, placing the order. (Session 1)
Server — the computer/program that receives requests, runs the backend logic, and prepares responses. The kitchen. (Session 1)
Database — where the data actually lives; the server queries it to fulfill requests. The fridge. (Session 1)
Endpoint — the specific URL where an API resource can be accessed; the stable part of the URL that doesn’t change from one request to the next (e.g., /v1/forecast). (Session 2, Part 3)

title: Glossary
text:
The Conversation — Requests & Responses
Request — the client asking for something. For our purposes, a request is written as a URL. (Session 1)
Response — what the server sends back: data, metadata, and a status code, almost always formatted as JSON. (Session 1)
HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) — the standard set of rules for sending requests and responses across the web. GET, POST, PUT, and DELETE are HTTP’s built-in verbs. (Session 2, Part 1)
HTTP Method — the verb of a request, announcing what kind of action it asks for: GET (read), POST (create), PUT/PATCH (update), DELETE (remove). (Session 2)
GET — the HTTP method for reading data. Parameters travel in the URL; nothing changes on the server. Nearly all data science API work is GET. (Session 2, Part 2)
POST — the HTTP method for sending new data to the server; the data travels in the request body rather than the URL. (Session 2, Part 2)
CRUD — the four fundamental operations: Create (POST), Read (GET), Update (PUT/PATCH), Delete (DELETE). (Session 2, Part 1)
Status Code — a number in every response saying what happened: 2xx success (200 OK), 4xx client-side problem (404 Not Found), 5xx server-side problem (500). (Session 1, Part 4)
Rate Limit — a cap on how many requests you may make in a time window; exceeding it returns status 429 Too Many Requests. (Session 1, Part 4)

title: Glossary
section: The Address — Anatomy of a URL
text:
The Address — Anatomy of a URL
URL (Uniform Resource Locator) — a web address: a single string that says exactly where a resource lives and how to reach it. For APIs, the URL is the request. (Session 2, Part 3)
Protocol — the first piece of a URL (https://): how to communicate. The s means secure. (Session 2, Part 3)
Base URL — the server’s address (api.open-meteo.com): who to talk to. (Session 2, Part 3)
Query String — everything after the ?: the key-value pairs that customize the request, chained together with &. (Session 2, Part 3)
Query Parameter — one key-value pair inside the query string, like latitude=35.28. (Session 2, Part 3)
API Key — an ID some APIs require as an extra query parameter (or header) to identify who is making the request — like showing a library card. Open-Meteo doesn’t need one. (Session 2, Part 3)

title: Glossary
text:
The Data — JSON
JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) — the plain-text format APIs use to send data: human-readable, machine-readable, and language-independent. No JavaScript knowledge required. (Session 1, Part 2)
Key / Value — the fundamental JSON pattern "key": value. The key is the label (always in double quotes); the value is the information — a string, number, boolean, array, or object. (Session 1, Part 2)
Object — a set of key-value pairs wrapped in curly braces { }. (Session 1, Part 2)
Array — an ordered list wrapped in square brackets [ ], like ["egg", "cheese"]. (Session 1, Part 2)
Nesting — an object or array sitting inside another object as a value, like "coordinates": { "lat": 35.28, "lon": -120.66 }. (Session 1, Part 2)
Body / Content — everything the server sends back in a response; the JSON wrapped in the outermost curly braces. (Session 1, Part 3)
Metadata — information about the response rather than the data itself: timestamps, units, generation time. (Session 1, Part 3)

title: Glossary
text:
In R
Named List — what a JSON object becomes in R: each key becomes a name, each nested object becomes a list inside the list. (Session 1, Part 2)
Parsing — converting the raw JSON text of a response into R data structures (e.g., with resp_body_json()). (Session 3)
Flattening — turning nested lists into a flat data frame (e.g., with as.data.frame()); nested keys join with periods, so coordinates → lat becomes the column coordinates.lat. (Session 1, Part 2)
httr2 — the R package we use to build and perform requests: request(), req_url_query(), req_perform(), resp_status(), resp_body_json(). (Session 3)

section: Part 1: What is an API? + The Data Flow
text:
Part 1: What is an API? + The Data Flow

Watch First: The Restaurant Analogy
Use the buttons to step through the animation — go at your own pace, pause, or replay any step.
Before you press anything, know what to look for. Two things only: who starts the exchange, and who you never talk to directly. Everything else is decoration.

  
    
      🙋Youthe Client
    
    ⇄
    
      🤵Waiterthe API
    
    ⇄
    
      👨‍🍳Kitchenthe Server
    
    ⇄
    
      🧊Fridgethe Database
    
  
  
  
    ⏮ Restart
    ◀ Back
    
    Next ▶
    ▶ Play
  





Now in Words
Here is the same story, written out:

You (the client) look at the menu and make a request — you place your order.
The waiter (the API) carries your request to the kitchen.
The kitchen (the server, with its fridge — the database) prepares your food.
The waiter brings back your meal (the response).

The key insight: you never walk into the kitchen yourself. The API is the controlled interface that lets you interact with the data source. And notice who starts everything: the client makes the request. Nothing happens until you order.






Important📖 Definition — API



An API (Application Programming Interface) is a structured way for one piece of software to request data or services from another — an agreed-upon set of rules that lets programs talk to each other without either one needing to know how the other works inside.


In data science, we use APIs to programmatically request data from external servers — weather services, sports databases, social media platforms, and more. (Every key term in this workshop is collected in the Glossary for quick reference.)






Tip🎯 Goal Check



In this analogy, our workshop goal is simply: place an order (make a request) and turn the meal that arrives (the response) into something we can analyze.



———————



Q1.
(Fill in the Blank): In the restaurant analogy, the waiter plays the role of the ________.






TipAnswer Q1





The API. The waiter is the go-between: it carries your request to the kitchen (server) and brings the response back to you (client).




———————


———————



Q2.
(Multiple Choice): What is the primary utility of a web API for a data analyst?

To create visual websites for data projects.
To store large CSV files in the cloud.
To design the database structure for a server.
To allow programmatic, repeatable, and direct access to live data from an external source.
To replace the need for any programming language.







TipAnswer Q2





d) An API provides a structured way for a program (like an R script) to directly request and receive live data, making data acquisition automated and scalable.




———————



The Data Flow — Same Story, Technical Names
Let’s go deeper into the architecture — same story as the restaurant, now with the technical names.


Watch First
Step through the request and response at your own pace — Next, Back, or press Play.
What to notice: the request makes exactly four stops — and the response comes back through the same stops in reverse. Count them as you click.



Now in Words
The animation traces a single API call from start to finish. There are four components in the chain: the Client (your R script or browser), the API (the “front door” of the data service), the Server (backend logic that processes the request), and the Database (where the actual data lives).
Request direction: Client (request) → API → Server → Database
Response direction: Client ← API ← Server (response) ← Database
The request moves left to right; the response travels the same path in reverse.






NoteKey Observations




The client is your R script or browser — anything making the request.
The API is the “front door” of the data service. (In Session 2 we’ll meet the endpoint — the exact address on that front door.)
The server processes the request and queries the database.
The response travels back the same path.
A client and server can exist on the same computer — this is common in local development.









Tip🎯 Goal Check



This chain is exactly what happens every time we run our workshop goal: the client (our R script) makes a request, and a response comes back for us to analyze.



———————



Visual Check — API Data Flow.
(Multiple Choice): In the animation, the API sits between the Client and the Server. What best describes the API’s role in this chain?

It stores the data permanently.
It runs the backend logic that queries the database.
It acts as a gateway — receiving requests from the client and routing them to the server.
It is the same as the database.
It draws the plots at the end of the analysis.







TipAnswer — Visual Check





c) The API is a gateway or controlled interface. It does not store data (that’s the database) and it does not run the core business logic (that’s the server). It is the stable “front door” that clients talk to, and it routes requests onward.




———————


———————



Q3.
(Fill in the Blank): A request travels: Client → ________ → Server → Database.






TipAnswer Q3





The API. The API always sits between the client and the server — requests go through it on the way in, and responses come back through it on the way out.




———————


———————



Q4.
(Fill in the Blanks — the restaurant story): Fill in each blank with one word from: client, waiter, kitchen, fridge, response.

I (the _____) look at the menu and place my order with the _____. My order is carried to the _____, which pulls ingredients from the _____. The finished dish comes back to my table — that dish is the _____.







TipAnswer Q4





I (the client) look at the menu and place my order with the waiter. My order is carried to the kitchen, which pulls ingredients from the fridge. The finished dish comes back to my table — that dish is the response.
(Translation: client → API → server → database → response.)




———————


———————



Q5.
(Multiple Choice — Callback to Q1): In the restaurant analogy, the API documentation is most analogous to:

The kitchen equipment
The cash register
The table number
The chef’s secret recipe book
The menu







TipAnswer Q5





e) The menu. Just like a menu tells you what’s available and how to order it, API documentation tells you what you can ask for and how to ask for it.




———————

title: Session 1: API Mechanics & Response Fundamentals
text:
Part 2: What is JSON?
Before we talk about what comes back from an API, we need a ten-minute detour. The responses we’ll be reading for the rest of this workshop are written in a format called JSON — so let’s meet it on its own first, before it shows up inside a response.






NoteWhy the Detour?



In the restaurant, the kitchen doesn’t hand you food in a random pile — every dish arrives plated in a predictable way. Data works the same way: servers send information back in one standard written format so that any program can read it. That format is JSON. Ten minutes here makes everything that follows easier.


Two ways through this part. Depending on how the hour is going, pick a tab: the Short Version covers everything in one example (~5 minutes); the Full Version adds the two hands-on activities (~15 minutes). Both paths end at the same weather JSON, and the questions afterward work for either one.

⚡ Short Version (~5 min)🧭 Full Version (~15 min)


JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is the plain-text format APIs use to send data. It’s human-readable, and every programming language — including R — can parse it. Don’t let the name worry you: no JavaScript required. And keep one distinction straight: the API is the waiter; JSON is the language the receipt is written in.
Everything you need to read JSON fits in this one restaurant order:
{
  "table": 7,
  "customer": {
    "name": "Maya",
    "rewards_member": true
  },
  "items": ["pancakes", "omelet", "coffee"],
  "total": 31.25
}
Four rules:

Every entry is a "key": value pair — keys always in double quotes, a colon between, commas separating the pairs
Values have types: strings in quotes ("Maya"), numbers bare (31.25), booleans bare and lowercase (true)
Curly braces { } make an object — a set of key-value pairs. customer is an object nested inside the order
Square brackets [ ] make an array — an ordered list. items holds three strings


Quick Check — Point and Read.
Together, point to: one key, one string, one number, one boolean, the array, and the nested object. Then answer: what is the value of "name", and where does it live?






TipAnswer — Point and Read





"Maya" — a string, living inside the nested customer object. (Top-level keys: table, customer, items, total; inside customer: name and rewards_member. The array is items; the boolean is true.)





The Payoff
Same structure, different keys — this is the shape of a real weather API response, and it’s exactly what our R script will receive tomorrow:
{
  "city": "San Luis Obispo",
  "coordinates": {
    "lat": 35.28,
    "lon": -120.66
  },
  "weather": {
    "main": "Clear",
    "temp": 72,
    "humidity": 45
  }
}
Nothing new: keys and values, with coordinates and weather as nested objects.




What is JSON?
JSON stands for JavaScript Object Notation. Don’t let the name scare you — you do not need to know JavaScript. JSON is just plain text, written with a few simple punctuation rules, used to describe structured data.
APIs almost universally speak JSON because it is:

Human-readable — you can open it and read it with your eyes
Machine-readable — every programming language (including R) can parse it
Language-independent — a Python server can send it and your R script can read it
Lightweight — it’s just text, so it travels fast







ImportantJSON is a Format, Not the API



Keep these two ideas separate: the API is the waiter — the messenger. JSON is the language the receipt is written in. When we say “the API returns JSON,” we mean: the messenger hands you a note, and the note is written in JSON.




Keys and Values
Here is a small, complete JSON example — a single breakfast order:
{
  "dish": "veggie omelet",
  "price": 12.50,
  "gluten_free": true
}
Every entry follows the same pattern: "key": value.

The key is the label — always wrapped in double quotes: "dish"
The value is the information itself, and how it’s written depends on its type:

Strings (text) are in quotes: "veggie omelet"
Numbers are bare: 12.50
Booleans (true/false) are bare and lowercase: true

A colon : connects each key to its value; commas separate the pairs
Curly braces { } wrap the whole thing



Objects, Arrays, and Nesting
Three more words of vocabulary and you can read almost any JSON in the wild:

An object is anything wrapped in curly braces { } — a set of key-value pairs. The breakfast order above is one object.
An array is an ordered list, wrapped in square brackets [ ] — like ["egg", "cheese", "spinach"].
Nesting means an object (or array) sitting inside another object, as a value.

All three in one order:
{
  "table": 7,
  "customer": {
    "name": "Maya",
    "rewards_member": true
  },
  "items": ["pancakes", "omelet", "coffee"],
  "total": 31.25
}
Read it out loud: table 7; the customer is a nested object with a name and a membership flag; the items are an array of three dishes; the total is a number. That’s it — that’s JSON.


———————


Guided Activity — Read the JSON.
Work through these together using the JSON below (~5 minutes):
{
  "name": "Avocado Toast",
  "category": "breakfast",
  "vegetarian": true,
  "calories": 350,
  "toppings": ["egg", "chili flakes"],
  "origin": {
    "country": "Australia",
    "decade": "2010s"
  }
}

How many key-value pairs are at the top level of this object?
What is the value of "vegetarian", and what type is it?
Which key holds an array? How many items does it have?
Which key holds a nested object?
What is the value of "country"?







TipAnswers — Read the JSON






Six: name, category, vegetarian, calories, toppings, origin.
true — a boolean (notice: no quotes around it).
toppings — an array with two items.
origin — its value is wrapped in its own curly braces { }.
"Australia" — a string, found inside the nested origin object.






———————


———————


Your Turn — Complete the JSON.
This JSON describes a coffee order, but it’s unfinished (~5 minutes). Fill in the three blanks with a value of the right type, then add one more key-value pair: "to_go" with the value true.
{
  "drink": "________",
  "size_oz": ____,
  "iced": ____,
  "flavors": ["vanilla", "caramel"]
}
As you write, check yourself against the rules: keys and strings get double quotes; numbers and booleans don’t; every pair except the last needs a comma after it.






TipOne Possible Answer — Complete the JSON





{
  "drink": "latte",
  "size_oz": 16,
  "iced": false,
  "flavors": ["vanilla", "caramel"],
  "to_go": true
}
Any drink string, any number, and either boolean works. The two things that matter: the types are right (quotes only around strings), and a comma was added after the flavors array before the new pair.





———————


From the Café to the API
Now the payoff. Here is the same structure with different keys — this is the shape of a real weather API response:
{
  "city": "San Luis Obispo",
  "coordinates": {
    "lat": 35.28,
    "lon": -120.66
  },
  "weather": {
    "main": "Clear",
    "temp": 72,
    "humidity": 45
  }
}
Nothing here is new: one object with keys and values, two of which (coordinates and weather) are nested objects. If you could read the avocado toast, you can read this — and this is exactly what will arrive every time our R script calls the weather API tomorrow.










ImportantThinking in R Terms



In R, a JSON object becomes a named list, and a JSON array becomes a vector or list. Nested objects become lists inside lists. When we flatten it all with as.data.frame(), nested keys become column names like coordinates.lat or weather.temp.








Tip🎯 Goal Check



Half of our goal is “format the response into something we can analyze.” You just did the first step by eye: reading JSON and finding the values you care about. Tomorrow, R does the same thing — just faster.



———————


Q6.
(Multiple Choice): The JSON data format, commonly used in API responses, organizes information using what fundamental structure?

Rows and columns
A nested series of bullet points
Key-value pairs
Formatted paragraphs of text
Comma-separated values







TipAnswer Q6





c) JSON data is built on key-value pairs (e.g., "city": "Chicago"), where a “key” is a string and a “value” can be a string, number, boolean, array, or another object.




———————


———————



Q7.
(Fill in the Blank): In R, a JSON object { } becomes a named ________.






TipAnswer Q7





A named list. Each JSON key becomes a name in the list, and nested JSON objects become lists inside the list.




———————


———————



Q8.
(Fill in the Blank — using the weather example above): If you flatten the weather JSON example with as.data.frame(), the column holding the latitude value would be named ________.






TipAnswer Q8





coordinates.lat — when R flattens nested JSON into a data frame, it joins the nested key names with a period. So coordinates → lat becomes coordinates.lat.




———————

title: Session 1: API Mechanics & Response Fundamentals
section: Part 3: Requests, Responses & the JSON Body
text:
Part 3: Requests, Responses & the JSON Body
Now let’s put the pieces together: the client sends a request, a response comes back (Part 1), and that response is written in JSON (Part 2). What does the whole response look like when we zoom out?

The Journey, One More Time
Here is the same request-and-response visual from Part 1 — replay it, but this time keep your eye on the return trip: the response leg is the part we dissect for the rest of this session.



Watch First
Step through the layers one at a time — each click reveals the next zone.
What to notice: the response has exactly three zones. As you click, ask of each zone: is this the data I wanted, information about the response, or the verdict on whether it worked?



Now in Words
The animation reveals the layers of a JSON response, one at a time:

The entire thing — everything the server sends back — is called the Body (or Content). It is wrapped in curly braces { }.
Inside that body, the content is divided into three zones:

Data: what we actually wanted (temperature, city name, coordinates)
Metadata: information about the response (timestamps, units)
Status code: tells us if the request worked


Take this slowly — this structure will show up in every response for the rest of the workshop. Now let’s define the two sides of the exchange precisely.


What is a Request?
A request is the client asking for information. Here is the one thing to remember today:

A request is written as a URL — a web address.

That’s it. When we want data from an API, we build a web address that describes what we want, and we send it. In Session 2 we will dissect exactly how that web address is put together, piece by piece.
(One aside for later: some APIs also ask you to include an ID called an API key — like showing a library card. The weather API we use in this workshop is free and doesn’t need one, so we can set that idea aside for now.)


What is a Response?
The server returns a response which contains:

Status code — tells you whether the request was successful (e.g., 200 OK)
Metadata — information about the response (timestamps, units, etc.)
Data — the actual information you requested (temperature, artist name, forecast, etc.)

This information is traditionally provided in JSON format — the format we just met in Part 2, laid out in the zones the animation just showed.


Look — an Actual Response
Enough diagrams: here is a real response from the exact weather API we’ll call tomorrow, with the three zones marked. This is not a simplified teaching example — this is what arrives on your screen.

  
    GET https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude=35.28&longitude=-120.66&current=temperature_2m&temperature_unit=fahrenheit
  
  
    ✅ Status code: 200 OK — the request worked (this rides along with the response)
  
  {
  "latitude": 35.25,
  "longitude": -120.75,
  "generationtime_ms": 0.027,
  "timezone": "America/Los_Angeles",
  "elevation": 96.0,
  "current_units": { "time": "iso8601", "temperature_2m": "°F" },
  "current": {
    "time": "2026-08-06T08:15",
    "temperature_2m": 61.9
  }
}
  
     Status code — did it work?
     Metadata — about the response
     Data — what we asked for
  

Read it with the anatomy in mind: the whole JSON body is wrapped in curly braces; the metadata zone describes the response (where, when, what units); the data zone — the current object — holds the one number we actually asked for: temperature_2m. The status code arrives alongside the body and tells us it all worked.






NoteYou Already Know How to Read This



Inside each zone it’s just what Part 2 taught: keys, values, and nesting. The anatomy here is about the zones — which keys are the data you wanted, which are information about the response, and which tell you whether it worked.








Tip🎯 Goal Check



Two halves of our goal, side by side: the request is a URL we send; the response is what we’ll format into something we can analyze. The response body is the raw material — our goal means taking this JSON and turning it into an R data frame.



———————



Q9.
(Fill in the Blank): A request is written as a ________ — a web address that asks the API for specific information.






TipAnswer Q9





A URL. That’s the entire request: a carefully built web address.




———————


———————



Q10.
(Multiple Choice): A response from an API contains which three things?

Data, metadata, and a status code
A URL, an API key, and a password
A plot, a table, and a summary
HTML, CSS, and JavaScript
Rows, columns, and cell values







TipAnswer Q10





a) A response contains the data you asked for, metadata about the response, and a status code that says whether the request worked.




———————


———————



Quick Checks — JSON Response Anatomy.
(Fill in the Blanks): One or two words each.

Everything the server sends back is called the body or content, and it is wrapped in curly ________.
The three zones inside the body are the data, the ________, and the status code.
The ______ ______ tells us whether the request worked.







TipAnswers — Quick Checks






Curly braces { }
The metadata
The status code





———————

title: Session 1: API Mechanics & Response Fundamentals
text:
Part 4: Status Codes

Look First
Status codes tell you what happened with your request. They are grouped by category:



Range
Category
Meaning




1xx
Informational
Request received, processing…


2xx
Success
Request was successful


3xx
Redirect
Resource moved to a different URL


4xx
Client Error
Something wrong with your request


5xx
Server Error
Something wrong on the server’s end



The most important ones for data work:

200 OK — Success! You got your data.
401 Unauthorized — Your credentials (e.g., an API key) are missing or invalid.
403 Forbidden — You don’t have permission to access this resource.
404 Not Found — The endpoint or resource doesn’t exist.
429 Too Many Requests — You’ve hit the rate limit.
500 Internal Server Error — The server broke; not your fault.







NotePractical Tip



In most data API work, your goal is to get a 200 response. If you don’t, the status code tells you where to look for the problem — your request (4xx) or their server (5xx).








Tip🎯 Goal Check



The status code is the first thing we check after making a request: a 200 means “the response arrived — go ahead and format it for analysis.”



———————



Q11.
(Fill in the Blank): A status code in the 4xx range means the mistake is on the ________ side; a 5xx code means the problem is on the ________ side.






TipAnswer Q11





4xx = the client side (you — your URL or request has a problem). 5xx = the server side (them — their system broke).




———————


———————



Q12.
(Multiple Choice): Your script fails with a 404 Not Found status code. What is the most likely source of the error?

The weather company’s server crashed.
Your internet is disconnected.
R is not installed correctly.
The database deleted your account.
The URL in your request is incorrect or misspelled.







TipAnswer Q12





e) A 404 Not Found is a client-side (4xx) error — you asked for a “page” that doesn’t exist on the server. The most likely culprit is a typo or mistake in the URL you built.




———————


———————



Q13.
(Multiple Choice — Callback to Q6): If you receive a response with a status code of 200 and the body contains JSON, which of the following would you expect to find in that response?

An error message explaining what went wrong
Key-value pairs containing the data you requested
A redirect URL to a different API
An empty response with no content
A request for payment







TipAnswer Q13





b) A 200 OK status means success, and the JSON body will contain the key-value pairs with the data you requested — temperature, coordinates, city name, etc.




———————

section: Part 1: Meet the Open-Meteo API + Browser Demo
text:
Part 1: Meet the Open-Meteo API + Browser Demo

Look First — A Real Request and a Real Response
Stop. This is the moment the last two sessions have been building toward. Here is a complete, real API request — and you can already read every piece of it from Session 2:
https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude=35.28&longitude=-120.66&current=temperature_2m&temperature_unit=fahrenheit
Before you run anything, inspect the URL: identify the endpoint, location, requested variable, and units. Then select Copy URL, paste it into a browser, and press Enter. The result is raw JSON.






ImportantInvestigate Before You Run



Predict what the server will return from the URL alone. Only then press Run in R. Keep the R console visible so everyone can see the request, status, and response.


{
  "latitude": 35.28,
  "longitude": -120.66,
  "timezone": "GMT",
  "current_units": { "time": "iso8601", "temperature_2m": "°F" },
  "current": {
    "time": "2026-08-06T16:00",
    "temperature_2m": 71.4
  }
}


Now in Words
For a day and a half, “request” and “response” have been arrows on a diagram. They just became real — and you did not write a single line of code. That was the payoff of Session 2’s URL anatomy: a request is just a URL — so a web browser can make one. Reading the URL piece by piece:

https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast — the endpoint (the stable front door)
? — “here come my details”
latitude=35.28&longitude=-120.66 — where (San Luis Obispo)
current=temperature_2m — what (the temperature right now)
temperature_unit=fahrenheit — how (in °F)

And every piece of the response is something you already know:

The endpoint and the query string in the address bar (?, &, key-value pairs) — Session 2
The response wrapped in curly braces { } — the body, in JSON — Session 1
Data (temperature_2m: 71.4) and metadata (current_units, timezone) — Session 1
Your browser made a GET request — typing a URL into the address bar is always a GET — Session 2

That number — 71.4 — is the actual temperature in San Luis Obispo right now. A server you’ve never seen just measured the world and handed you the answer, because you asked correctly.
Change the coordinates to Boston (42.36, -71.06) and reload. Ask: How does its weather compare with San Luis Obispo? This is the question we will answer across cities and dates.


About This API
We will use Open-Meteo for the rest of the workshop — a free weather API built for exactly this kind of learning:

No sign-up. No API key. No credit card. You can start making requests immediately.
The main endpoint is https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast — the endpoint from Session 2: the stable “front door” that never changes. Everything else we want (which city, which measurements, which units) goes in the query string.







NoteWhy api.open-meteo.com and Not Just open-meteo.com?



Notice the endpoint is not the same address as the regular website. Open-Meteo actually has two front doors:

open-meteo.com — the door for humans: a web page with documentation, meant to be read in a browser.
api.open-meteo.com — the door for programs: a server whose only job is to answer requests with raw JSON data.

Putting the API on its own api. subdomain is a near-universal convention — it lets the company run, scale, and update the data service separately from the marketing/docs website. When you see api. at the front of a domain, you’re looking at the machine door, not the human one. Keep this in mind: later today we’ll meet a third door for a different service.








NoteWhat About API Keys, Clients & Secrets?



Many commercial APIs (OpenWeather, X, Spotify, …) require you to register and receive credentials — an API key, sometimes a client ID and secret — which you attach to every request like an ID card, and which you must store carefully (never directly in your script!). It’s an important real-world concept, and the Practice Labs on this site show it in action.
But today we get to skip all of it. Open-Meteo is free and open — so we can spend our hour on the actual skill: requests and responses.








Important🎯 The Goal — Half Met Already



Read the goal sentence again: “Make a request to an API, then format the response into something we can analyze.”

Make a request to an API — ✅ you just did it. That URL was the request.
Get a response — ✅ you just did that too. That JSON was the response.

With zero lines of code, the request/response loop from Sessions 1 and 2 just happened for real, on your screen. So what’s left for R? Automation. The browser can make one request at a time, by hand, and you have to read the JSON with your eyes. R will do exactly the same thing the browser just did — same URL, same GET, same JSON — but it can do it a hundred times in a loop and hand the answers back as data you can analyze. That’s the entire rest of the workshop: not a new idea, just automating the thing you just did.



———————



Q1.
(Fill in the Blank): The stable part of the URL — https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast — that never changes from one request to the next is called the ________.






TipAnswer Q1





The endpoint. The changing part (after the ?) is the query string.




———————


———————



Q2.
(Multiple Choice): Which statement about the Open-Meteo API is true?

It requires a paid subscription.
It requires an API key stored in .Renviron.
It is free and requires no API key at all.
It only works inside Positron.
It only returns data for cities in Europe.







TipAnswer Q2





c) Open-Meteo is free and open — no key, no registration. (Many other APIs do require a key; that’s the “ID card” concept from the callout above.)




———————


———————



Q3.
(Fill in the Blank): When you paste the request URL into a browser, what comes back is not a web page — it is raw ________.






TipAnswer Q3





JSON — the same body/content structure we studied in Session 1.




———————


———————



Q4.
(Multiple Choice): Typing a URL into the browser’s address bar and pressing Enter performs which kind of HTTP request?

POST
DELETE
PUT
PATCH
GET







TipAnswer Q4





e) The address bar always makes a GET request — you are reading data, exactly like our R scripts will.




———————
